rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: What play store reviews say about support

Hi {first_name},

I read 300 recent smallcase Google Play reviews (India storefront, collected 2026-10-20). Of the negative ones, 7.6% cite the support channel failing (no response, an unanswered ticket, repeated follow-up) rather than the product itself.

Treat it as directional. App reviews skew toward angry customers, this is a single snapshot, and I have no contact volume data. Does 7.6% look anywhere near your internal picture?

I work on conversational AI for BFSI support. We ran bots against 18 real support queries from this domain, and I can send you the query set and the 8 cases where a naive retrieval bot was confidently wrong. You can keep them whether or not you reply.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats and the offer is real, but the 7.6% is a modest number with no hook, and the recipient has little reason to care or reply.
failures: The email's own caveats undercut the headline: 7.6% of negative reviews is small, and 'does it look near your internal picture' invites a shrug. Lead with something more striking from the brief, such as the verbatim quote about a ticket unresolved for 45 days (TKT-143999), which is checkable on the Play Store and far more vivid.

The denominator is ambiguous: '300 recent reviews' then '7.6% of the negative ones' never says how many were negative or substantive (66 negative of 121 substantive). The recipient cannot reproduce 7.6% in ten minutes without that. State the 66 and 121 as the brief gives them.

No insight is offered about their operation. The brief's strongest finding, that deflection rates were near-identical (67% vs 72%) while correctness differed hugely (39% vs 94%), is absent. Add a line connecting it to the support-channel failures, e.g. that automation volume hides wrong answers.

The offer says 'the 8 cases where a naive retrieval bot was confidently wrong' but never says what the bot's outcome was elsewhere, so the offer feels like a teaser. Name one concrete thing they get (query set, the 8 cases, the routing-vs-retrieval comparison).
'I work on conversational AI for BFSI support' is a generic sales-ish identifier. Replace it with what was actually done: the eval on 18 real queries, and say who ran it.
Subject line 'What play store reviews say about support' is generic and does not name smallcase. Name the company.
'Does 7.6% look anywhere near your internal picture?' is a fair question, but the stacked caveat sentence reads defensive. Compress it to one clause.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: Smallcase: ticket TKT-143999, 45 days on

Hi {first_name},

A 1-star Google Play review of smallcase reads: "raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution." It is one of 66 negative reviews among 121 with substantive text (300 fetched, India storefront, 2026-10-20). 7.6% of those negative reviews cite the support channel failing rather than the product. Does that match what you see internally? It is directional only: reviews skew angry, it is one snapshot, and I have no contact volumes.

I ran 18 real support queries from this domain through two bot setups. Deflection was near-identical, 67% vs 72%, but correct disposal was 39% vs 94%, so automation volume can hide wrong answers. I can send the 18-query set and the 8 cases where the retrieval bot was confidently wrong, yours to keep.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats and it ships, but it is a dense stat paragraph followed by a loosely connected bot eval, at about 128 words just under the limit.
failures: Subject 'ticket TKT-143999, 45 days on' implies the ticket is still open today. The brief only shows the reviewer saying 45 days at the time of writing, and another quoted review says the team called after the Google Play review. Reword to 'a 45-day-old ticket in a Play review' or similar.

The two paragraphs are not connected. Say in one line why retrieval-bot confident-wrongness matters for support-channel failures like the quoted ticket, or the eval reads as a pitch bolted onto a review stat.

The first paragraph packs sample size, storefront, date and fetch count into a parenthetical. Cut '300 fetched' and the date parenthetical, or move them to the offer, to relieve density and the 128-word body that sits close to the cap.
'Does that match what you see internally?' is a weak, generic question. Ask something only a support head could answer, such as whether tickets stall at the handoff or inside the queue.
Offer the review quotes and the review-sampling method as well, so the verifiable half of the email is also something they keep.

rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats, with a real offer and a checkable smallcase-specific opener, but the link from one stalled ticket to the deflection-vs-correctness point is loose and the middle paragraph reads slightly like a pivot to a pitch.
failures: 'On 18 real queries' does not say the queries are not smallcase's. A hostile reader may assume they are, or ask why they should care. Say 'from this domain' or 'wealth-app support queries' to prevent a misread.
The jump from 'tickets stall' to 'a bot that answers wrongly still counts as deflected' is not earned. Add a short bridge on why a wrong-but-closed ticket would not show up in their queue metrics.
'I work on conversational AI for BFSI support' is a generic credential line. Cut it or replace it with something specific about what was built or measured.

The 7.6% has no base. The recipient cannot tell if it is 5 reviews or 50 without opening the review set. Offering the sampling method helps, but naming the 66 negative reviews would make the figure honest at a glance.
'so only you can say' is slightly coy. Ask the handoff-vs-queue question once and plainly.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: A ticket 45 days old

Hi {first_name},

A public Play Store review of smallcase reads: "Customer service can be improved. CC is acting only as postman, raised issue 45 days back, TKT-143999, still no resolution."

This class of complaint is rarely a product gap. It usually means the handoff between support and whoever can fix the issue is failing, so check ticket age by resolving team, not by queue.

Among the negative reviews I looked at, 7.6% cite the support channel failing. Reviews skew angry and I have no contact volumes, so treat that as directional.

I work on conversational AI for BFSI support. I can send the 18-query set and the 8 cases where a naive bot was confidently wrong, whether or not you reply.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats, with a real checkable quote and a genuine offer, but the insight is an unproven assertion and the offer is buried and slightly mismatched to the opening.
failures: 'This class of complaint is rarely a product gap. It usually means the handoff... is failing' is asserted as fact with no support in the brief. It is a generality, not a claim about smallcase, so it is not a hard fail, but a hostile reader will challenge it. Soften to 'often reads as' or tie it to what the quote itself says (CC 'acting only as postman').

The advice 'check ticket age by resolving team, not by queue' is presented as a prescription without evidence. It is plausible but untested in the brief. Frame it as a suggestion from experience, not a rule.

The offer (18-query set and 8 confidently-wrong cases) is about naive bot failure, but the email never says what the eval measured or why it connects to a handoff problem. The link between a 45-day-old ticket and a bot's confident wrong answers is unexplained, so the offer feels bolted on. Add one sentence: a bot that deflects at the same rate but is wrong 8 times creates exactly this kind of stuck ticket. Only use figures the brief states.
'The 8 cases' appears without context. State that the 18 queries are real support queries from this domain, as the brief says, so the recipient knows what they would receive.
'I looked at' is vague about method. Say 'Play Store reviews' once more clearly, since the sample is app reviews only, which is the caveat that matters most.
'Whether or not you reply' is fine, but 'I work on conversational AI for BFSI support' is a generic sales-sounding self-description. Replace with what you actually did, e.g. built and ran the eval.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: Support-channel share of negative reviews

Hi {first_name},

In 300 recent Google Play reviews of Upstox (India storefront, collected 2026-10-20), 6.5% of the negative ones cite the support channel failing, such as no reply to a ticket or repeated follow-ups, rather than the product itself. You can check it against the public reviews in ten minutes.

It is directional only. I have no contact volume, it is a single snapshot, and app reviews skew toward angry customers. I'd be curious whether it matches your internal picture.

I work on conversational AI for support in Indian BFSI. We ran 18 real support queries from this domain through a naive retrieval bot, and it was confidently wrong 8 times. I'm happy to send the 18-query set and those 8 cases whether or not you reply.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Factually clean and honest about its limits, but it hands a senior operator a small number (6.5%) with no framing for why it matters, then pivots to an eval result that is not connected to Upstox's problem, so it is likely to be read and deleted.
failures: The 6.5% figure is low and the draft gives no reason a recipient should care. It does not say that this share is about the support channel failing rather than the product, and that this is the slice a bot can or cannot fix. Frame why this specific slice matters, without adding any new numbers.

The bridge from the review stat to the 18-query eval is missing. 'I work on conversational AI' followed by a bot being wrong 8 times reads like two separate emails. Connect them in one sentence: the eval shows that automation rate alone hides wrong answers, which is relevant to a channel where customers already report no reply.

The brief has real customer quotes (e.g. 'no reply on mail or ticket', the bank account change complaint with repeated emails and documents already sent). The draft uses none. One quoted line would make this clearly about Upstox and not a template with a number swapped in.

The eval's actual insight is omitted. Near-identical deflection (67% vs 72%) with very different correctness (39% vs 94%) is the non-obvious point. The draft only gives the failure half. Adding the 'similar deflection, different correctness' framing would raise insight, using only figures in the brief's form.

'You can check it against the public reviews in ten minutes' is fine, but the draft does not say how (Play Store, India storefront, sort by recent, filter 1-2 stars). A concrete method line would strengthen verifiability.

'I'd be curious whether it matches your internal picture' is a soft, generic closer. Replace it with a specific question tied to the data, e.g. whether tickets like account or bank detail changes are where follow-ups pile up.
Sender identity is a bare {sender} placeholder with no role or company. Make sure it is filled in before sending.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: when the support channel is the complaint

Hi {first_name},

6.5% of negative Upstox reviews on the Play Store (India storefront, 300 recent reviews, fetched 2026-10-20) cite the support channel failing, not the product. One reads: "no reply on mail or ticket". To check, sort by recent and filter to 1-2 stars. It is directional only: no contact volume, one snapshot, and reviews skew angry.

I work on conversational AI for support in Indian BFSI. In our 18-query eval, a naive retrieval bot and a routed, integrated one automated 67% and 72%, but disposed 39% and 94% correctly. Where customers already report no reply, a confident wrong answer is the bigger risk. I can send the 18 queries and the 8 wrong cases either way.

Is it tickets like bank detail changes where follow-ups pile up?

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Clean on facts and caveats, with a real offer and no meeting ask, so it can ship; it's a solid 3-ish email whose weak spots are an unexplained small base and a closing question that guesses from one review.
failures: The 6.5% is a share of the 46 negative reviews, but the sentence reads as if the base were the 300 fetched reviews. Say 'of 46 negative reviews' (the brief's number) so a skeptical reader doesn't discover the small base themselves. Don't convert it into a count.

The closing question 'tickets like bank detail changes' rests on one unquoted review. Either quote that review's bank-account-change complaint or soften the guess, because the recipient can't verify it from the email.
At roughly 126 words it sits just under the 130 cap. Cut 'To check,' or merge the two eval sentences to leave headroom for edits.

The 'confident wrong answer is the bigger risk' line is opinion linked to the review stat. Make the link explicit: the 8 wrong cases came from the naive bot, not from Upstox's systems, so the draft doesn't imply otherwise.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: a 1-star review that isn't about the app

Hi {first_name},

"no reply on mail or ticket, worst service" is a 1-star Upstox review on the India Play Store.

A complaint about the support channel itself usually points to a handoff failing between the ticket queue and the team that owns the action, such as an account closure. It is not a feature gap, so it won't show in roadmap data. Check whether tickets needing another team's action have a named owner after the first reply.

Across 300 recent reviews, 6.5% of the negative ones cite this. Reviews skew angry and I have no contact volumes, so treat it as directional.

I work on conversational AI for BFSI support. I can send the 18-query set and the 8 cases where a naive bot was confidently wrong, whether or not you reply.

{sender}
unsupported_claims: usually points to a handoff failing between the ticket queue and the team that owns the action, such as an account closure
It is not a feature gap, so it won't show in roadmap data.
rounds.verdict: Honest numbers and a real offer, but it asserts an unsupported root cause (a handoff failure between the queue and an owning team) as if it were known, so it cannot ship.
failures: Remove or hedge the causal diagnosis. The brief shows tickets going unanswered and repeated follow-ups, not a handoff between the queue and an owning team. Stating it as what the pattern 'usually points to' is a plausible but unsupported claim about how Upstox operates.

The account-closure example is only partly grounded. The quoted review says 'no help to close account', but the draft ties it to a team-ownership mechanism the data does not show. Cite only what the review says.
'It won't show in roadmap data' is an assertion about Upstox's internal tooling and planning. Cut it, or reframe it as a question rather than a statement.

'Check whether tickets needing another team's action have a named owner' is advice built on the unsupported diagnosis. It reads as prescriptive and a little presumptuous to a senior operator. Replace it with something drawn from the brief, such as the eval finding that near-identical deflection rates hid very different correctness (67% vs 72% automated, 39% vs 94% correct).

The 6.5% figure is stated correctly as 'of the negative ones', but the 46-of-102 base is not given, so the reader cannot check it. Add the base in the brief's own terms, without converting it into a count of reviews.

The subject line promises 'a 1-star review that isn't about the app', but the quote itself is mostly about the support channel and also mentions the user opening a Zerodha account. Consider whether naming a competitor-switch signal would be stronger, using only what the quote says.
The offer is good ('whether or not you reply'). Make it more concrete by saying the 18 queries come from this domain and what the confidently-wrong cases show, using only the brief's facts.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: a 1-star review that ends at a competitor

Hi {first_name},

A 1-star Upstox review on the India Play Store reads: "no reply on mail or ticket, worst service, opening zerodha account".

This class of complaint is about how a request ended, so the number to check is how many contacts end correctly, not how many end without an agent. In our eval on 18 real support queries from this domain, one bot automated 67% and another 72%, yet they disposed 39% and 94% correctly. The first was confidently wrong 8 times.

On your side, 6.5% of negative reviews cite the support channel failing. That is from 300 recent reviews, 102 with substantive text, 46 of those negative. I have no contact volumes and reviews skew angry, so it is directional only.

I work on conversational AI for BFSI support. I can send the 18 queries and the 8 confidently-wrong cases, whether or not you reply.

{sender}
rounds.verdict: Facts all trace to the brief and the offer is real, but the body runs about 149 words against a 130 limit, so it cannot ship until trimmed.
failures: Cut about 20+ words to get under 130. Merge the sample-size sentence into the 6.5% sentence, e.g. '6.5% of 46 negative reviews (from 102 substantive of 300) cite the support channel failing; no contact volumes, reviews skew angry, directional only.'
Delete or shorten 'This class of complaint is about how a request ended, so the number to check is...'. It is the longest sentence and is abstract framing.

The quoted review is about no reply at all, while the eval is about wrong disposal. The link between them is asserted rather than shown. Say plainly that a closed-wrong ticket and an unanswered ticket look the same to the customer.
Mention that the review data is a single snapshot, since the brief lists it as a known gap and the draft omits it.
Name what the two bots were (naive retrieval vs routing plus system integration). 'One bot... another' hides the one detail a practitioner would want.
'I work on conversational AI for BFSI support' is a generic sales line. Cut it or replace it with something specific.

rounds.draft:
SUBJECT: a review about repeated emails

Hi {first_name},

An Upstox Play Store reviewer wrote: "kitne Mail upstox ko bhej chuka hun unhone Jo document mange voh bhi Main send kar chuka hun".

A wrongly closed ticket and an unanswered one look the same to the customer, so check closed tickets with repeat contacts, not just unanswered ones.

In our 18-query eval, a naive retrieval bot automated 67% but disposed 39% correctly, and was confidently wrong 8 times. Routing plus system integration automated 72% and disposed 94% correctly, with 0 confidently wrong.

On Upstox, 6.5% of negative reviews cite the support channel failing. It is a single snapshot with no contact volumes, and reviews skew angry, so it is directional only.

I run these evals on BFSI support queries. The 18 queries and 8 failure cases are yours either way.

{sender}
unsupported_claims: A wrongly closed ticket and an unanswered one look the same to the customer, so check closed tickets with repeat contacts, not just unanswered ones.
The 18 queries and 8 failure cases are yours either way.
rounds.verdict: The quote and eval numbers are accurate, but the email implies the reviewer's ticket was wrongly closed (the brief says nothing about closure), and the 'check closed tickets' advice rests on that invented premise, so it cannot ship as written.
failures: The line about a 'wrongly closed ticket' implies Upstox closes tickets wrongly. The quote only says the customer sent multiple emails and documents. Nothing in the brief says any ticket was closed. Rewrite so it says only what the quote shows: repeated contact and documents already sent.

The insight (closed tickets with repeat contacts) is the writer's inference, not a measured finding. Either label it as a hypothesis ('my guess is...') or drop it. As written it reads as a diagnosis of Upstox's operation.

The quote is truncated mid-sentence and stitched together, and it drops the context (primary bank account change). Quote it faithfully, or use the full available fragment, so the recipient can find it in ten minutes.

The 6.5% line is placed after the eval numbers and the caveats are bolted on in a clipped form. Say it is 6.5% of negative reviews in a 300-review India Play Store snapshot, so the recipient can verify the scope.

The offer ('The 18 queries and 8 failure cases are yours either way') is a concrete offer, but 'either way' is vague about mechanism. State how they get it, e.g. 'reply and I'll send them', so the offer is actionable. Also, '8 failure cases' is the 8 confidently-wrong instances, so name them as such.
The eval paragraph (67% vs 72%, 39% vs 94%) is not connected to the Upstox quote. Add a clause tying it to the repeat-contact pattern, or the email feels like two separate pitches.
'I run these evals on BFSI support queries' is a generic credential. Say what the 18 queries were drawn from, within what the brief supports (real support queries from this domain).
